title: Board of County Commissioners — Sep 30, 2026
recap:
This was a work session — no formal votes were taken. The morning focused entirely on the Employee Housing Impact Mitigation Fee. Staff presented the formula, fee history, and regional comparisons. The county has collected roughly $4.4 million since major fee adjustments in 2022, averaging about $1 million a year — well short of the estimated $4 million annual target needed to bond for affordable housing construction. No units have been built with those funds yet; the county is still in planning and infrastructure assessment stages.

Public comment ran long and was largely critical. Residents, real estate professionals, builders, and attorneys cited the outdated 2000 employee generation study, a steep jump in the affordability gap (from $527 to $1,112 per square foot since 2022), declining vacant land sales, and a chilling effect on construction — particularly for local families building primary homes. Suggestions included raising the 2,000-square-foot threshold before fees kick in, smoothing the rate curve, deferring or forgiving fees for full-time local residents, incentivizing deed-restricted ADU construction, and pursuing private-public development partnerships. An attorney noted a challenge to the fee structure is pending at the Colorado Supreme Court. Commissioners signaled openness to revisions and committed to a future decision-making meeting.

In the afternoon, commissioners reviewed 13 CCI legislative proposals for the 2027 session. No binding positions were set; Commissioner Gleason was authorized to vote on Friday with flexibility to adjust based on floor discussion. Tentative leanings included support for AI/data-privacy modernization, ground ambulance billing reform, and HUTF rural funding negotiations; lukewarm support for online legal notice publication; and opposition or abstention on several others including autopsy record changes, unfunded mandate study committees, and a Medicaid expansion for justice-involved individuals.

On community support grants: the Telluride Historical Museum was tentatively approved at $2,500 (down from the $5,000 request, reflecting prior funding history). The Telluride Environmental Science and Engineering Laboratory request for $10,000 was continued pending a presentation from the project team; commissioners want clarity on deliverables and actual partnerships before committing funds. The Telluride Junior Nordic Ski Program equipment request was denied, consistent with past precedent on capital and gear funding.

title: Town Council (Special) — Sep 30, 2026
recap:
Council met in special session to hear an appeal of the Planning and Zoning Commission's unanimous July 23 approval of a preliminary large-scale subdivision to consolidate two lots — Lot 34 and Lot 34B — into a single parcel at 700 West Pacific Avenue (the Carhenge lot). Three council members were recused due to proximity to the property, leaving a four-member quorum.

Appellants argued that the town attorney never performed a required gatekeeping review of whether the applicant had authority to submit the application under the Bachmann Village covenants, that 17 of 23 subdivision design criteria were improperly bypassed, and that a pending HARC application showed development was in fact being proposed. Staff and the applicant's attorney countered that covenants are a private matter outside the land use code, that staging applications is lawful, and that inapplicable criteria are not waived. Acting town attorney advised that no written town-attorney sign-off is required under the code.

Council voted 3-1 to affirm the PNZ decision. The dissenting member expressed concern that the Bachmann Village covenants were not factored into PNZ's factual basis. Council directed special counsel to draft a resolution memorializing the decision.

votes.item: Affirm PNZ approval — Carhenge lot consolidation

title: HARC — Sep 30, 2026

For Buildings A, B, and C (along the river), HARC directed the applicant to significantly reduce mass and scale, eliminate the loft level on Building C, step down facades more intentionally, reduce glazing on specific elevations, and add a dedicated pedestrian bridge per Accommodations Policy 6.

All three votes were unanimous.

title: Board of Trustees — Sep 29, 2026
recap:
The board held its first budget hearing for the 2027 fiscal year. Staff flagged a larger-than-expected sales tax decline, attributed partly to a slowdown in building permits and the wind-down of a major local project. The budget is described as conservative, with possible draws on reserves if the board later prioritizes a master plan or avalanche study. Grant funding for either item may also be pursued if opportunities arise.

A $25,000 placeholder was included in the Rico Center grant line for back-stair repairs and AV equipment replacement. The board discussed combining maintenance and grooming positions and explored a volunteer grooming program for the coming winter.

The board directed staff to bring numbers to first reading on a pay increase for town marshals — options discussed included a $5/hour raise for the senior marshal and adding paid travel time for both officers. No vote was taken.

On the water fund, staff detailed the condition of an aging storage tank, with restoration quotes ranging from roughly $50,000 to $70,000. Two vendors offered to split payment across two budget cycles at no additional cost. A Silver Creek design-engineering grant previously expected did not materialize; staff is monitoring for the funding to reopen.

title: BOCC — Sep 29, 2026
recap:
Ouray County held its second 2027 budget work session, working through department spending plans aimed at closing a roughly $1.5–1.6 million general fund deficit. No formal votes were taken; commissioners gave direction to department heads and the county manager on bottom-line budgets, with a formal adoption meeting set for December 8.

EMS presented the largest single development: a restructured budget that eliminates the general fund transfer entirely for 2027 — saving approximately $155,000 — through a revised billing matrix, moving employees onto Ridgway Fire's health insurance plan, and zeroing out the ambulance barn lease after Ouray Fire agreed to provide bay access at no cost.

Land use was directed to meet the 15% reduction target even if it requires reducing staff hours or eliminating a position, with the county manager to work out specifics. A fee schedule update covering building permits (a ~29% inflation adjustment), land use permits, short-term rental renewals (proposed increase from $235 to $400), and road impact fees was authorized to proceed to a hearing.

The assessor, clerk/elections, treasurer, public health, IT/GIS, road and bridge, and human services budgets were reviewed and accepted as placeholders pending final reconciliation. Commissioners discussed including the BOCC share in the cost allocation to road and bridge (potentially ~$200,000), directing staff to verify feasibility. A sheriff's office work session is scheduled for the following Tuesday, following a Monday joint session with the City of Ouray on a proposed law enforcement cooperation agreement.

title: San Miguel County 5x5 Meeting — Sep 24, 2026
recap:
San Miguel County hosted the regional 5x5 meeting, bringing together commissioners and staff from Archuleta, Dolores, Montezuma, La Plata, and San Miguel counties, along with state and federal legislative representatives.

Wildfire dominated the discussion. Counties shared experiences from a brutal season — a 1,700-acre fire in Archuleta, the roughly 90,000-acre Ferris fire in Dolores — and compared strategies including water-storage tanks, Pano AI detection cameras, and defensible-space funding gaps. Montezuma County announced it is using Title III SRS funds to install two Pano cameras at Park Point in partnership with Mesa Verde National Park. San Miguel noted its cameras have already enabled early response. Pitkin County is reportedly developing legislation for statewide Pano funding; Proposition 137 on the November ballot would direct sporting-goods sales tax toward wildfire prevention and watershed restoration.

San Miguel County reported an 870-unit housing deficit projected to exceed 1,000 units by 2030. A citizen stakeholder group has completed a package of land-use code changes for planning commission and commissioner review. The county also adopted the Colorado model low-energy and carbon building code. A CDOT partnership at the Draco shop site targets 12 initial workforce-housing units, expandable to 46 if a wastewater plant is built. The county is re-advertising for a planning director after the first round yielded no suitable hire.

La Plata County updated two Urban Renewal Authority projects: up to 135 housing units with a childcare facility on Florida Road, and a redevelopment study of the Durango Mall area. A Region 9 broadband grant of $823,000 was approved for the Wolf Creek fiber project, adding redundant connectivity for Archuleta County. La Plata and Archuleta counties jointly filed a complaint with the PUC over repeated fiber cuts by Lumen Technologies that knock out 911 services.

State Representative Stewart highlighted a new treatment-in-place law allowing EMS reimbursement under Medicaid without hospital transport, effective January 1, 2027, with commercial-plan expansion under study. Senator Hickenlooper's office flagged the Fix Our Forest Act (passed Senate committee), the 340B rural hospital prescription drug bill, and concern over a proposed OMB rule that would let agencies terminate federal grants without notice. The group agreed by consensus to extend standing invitations to the Southern Ute Indian Council and Ute Mountain Ute Tribe for future 5x5 meetings.

title: Planning & Zoning — Sep 24, 2026
recap:

The proposal calls for four duplex buildings — eight one-bedroom units on a 0.91-acre site — which is within both the IGA's cap of ten units and the zone district's density limits. The commission directed staff to convene a small working group — including arborists, a HARC member, and public works representation — to identify specific code problems before a draft amendment comes forward, likely in November.

title: Mountain Village Town Council — Sep 17, 2026
recap:
Council approved two proclamations: one designating September 2026 as Suicide Prevention Month, and a second — added from the dais after a resident's comment — proclaiming September 11th as Patriot Day and Day of Remembrance.

On the consent agenda, minutes and the Telluride Foundation agency funding agreement passed without discussion. An improvement and maintenance agreement with the Cortina Land Condominium Owners Association — settling a dispute over road and utility responsibility — was pulled for discussion and passed 5-1. Jennifer Vogel was appointed to a four-year term on the Telluride Regional Airport Authority through September 2030. Patrick Latcham was appointed as the TMVOA representative to the Plaza Vending Committee.

Council passed second reading of an ordinance amending the municipal code governing the Public Art Commission, moving operational details from code into bylaws. A companion resolution adopting those bylaws — replacing a staff seat with a business-community appointee — also passed.

No vote was taken; staff will develop a preferred alternative and bring a formal resolution to initiate the entitlement process.

title: SSR (Strategic Stakeholder Roundtable) — Sep 15, 2026
recap:
The group's eighth meeting focused on proposed land use code changes aimed at making affordable and workforce housing easier to build in San Miguel County. Staff walked through previously discussed items — revised minimum lot sizes (2 acres for low density, half-acre for medium density, no minimum for high density), reduced building setbacks from 12.5 to 10 feet, streamlined one- and two-step review tiers for projects with significant deed restrictions, and expanded ADU and caretaker unit allowances.

The bulk of the meeting centered on the Community Housing (CH) zone. The central question was whether to set a unit cap above which a project would require the full five-step PUD process. After extended discussion, voting members reached a rough consensus — though not the full 70% supermajority — around 175 units as that trigger, with one member dissenting in favor of a higher cap. Staff noted the recommendation is nonbinding and will be passed to the Planning Commission and Board of County Commissioners.

The group also flagged two items for future meetings: whether to raise the 30% housing mitigation requirement for high-density free-market development (which may require a new linkage study), and whether the September 30th impact mitigation fee session could open that conversation.

votes.item: Cap on CH zone units before PUD required

title: San Miguel County Planning Commission — Sep 10, 2026
recap:
The commission worked through three land use code amendments, each recommended to the BOCC by unanimous vote.

Forestry Practices (new Section 6-4): Adds a regulatory framework focused on surface disturbance rather than board feet. Key thresholds: activities under 1.5 acres are exempt; 1.5–80 acres is minor (administrative); over 80 acres is major (two-step Planning Commission/BOCC review). Qualifying wildfire mitigation work done under West Region Wildfire Council or Colorado State Forest Service operates under a general permit. The commission added language on aerial resources (replacing "aerial extraction"), clarified streamside management zone buffers, and required emergency preparedness plans to explicitly address red flag warnings and fire restrictions.

Oil & Gas Operations (new Section 6-5): Replaces existing Section 5-26. All operations move to two-step review. Written notice to neighbors increased from 20 to 30 days. A 500-foot riparian/water-body buffer was added. Visual quality language was amended to require no adverse road impacts.

Deep Geothermal Operations (new Section 6-6): Entirely new regulations. Two-step review required. Residential setback set at 1,000 feet (up from a draft 500 feet), with a 500-foot buffer added for riparian areas. Continuous seismic monitoring required for injection wells. A related amendment broadens the data-center renewable-energy provision to cover all Article 6 energy sources, not just solar.

title: Ouray County BOCC — Sep 9, 2026
recap:
The board held a work session with Rural Homes nonprofit developer Paul Nager on the status of Waterview Homes Phase 2 in Ouray. Phase 1's 21 homes are fully occupied, including two units operating as licensed home-based childcare centers — both reported successful. Phase 2 is platted for roughly 42 units but faces several hurdles: a $1.9 million state loan due July 2027, a pending $1.4 million congressional-directed HUD grant whose terms are not yet finalized, and the need for new city water and sewer capacity. Next steps include a community/city work session to assess rental vs. ownership mix and market absorption.

The board then received a detailed budget overview from Finance Director Jason, projecting a roughly $1.5 million general fund structural deficit for 2027 — about 15% of general fund spending. Personnel represents approximately 70% of general fund expenditures. Department heads' combined proposed cuts reached only about $80,000, or 3% of operating costs. Options discussed included reducing hours from 40 to 36 for applicable employees (~$275,000 savings), furlough days tied to the 13 county holidays (~$260,000), a 1% merit bonus elimination (~$43,000), retirement contribution reductions (~$45,000–50,000 per percentage point), and benefit plan analysis. Staff and commissioners acknowledged that reduction in force remains a likely outcome.

Commissioners agreed on a budget process: department-by-department work sessions on September 23rd and a special session September 29th to set top-line department allocations, a preliminary budget presentation October 13th, and budget adoption targeted for December 8th.

In admin reports, County Manager Mendez announced the hire of Henry Mitchell as the county's new Recovery Manager, beginning September 28th. A TABOR notice for the November disaster sales tax ballot measure is active; pro/con statements are due to the county manager by noon September 18th.

title: Board of County Commissioners — Sep 9, 2026
recap:
Commissioners reviewed Colorado's November ballot measures and staked out positions. They agreed to oppose the constitutional right to natural gas (formerly Initiative 177), oppose the income tax rate cap, support the graduated income tax amendment (Amendment 87), support the TABOR revenue cap increase for K-12 education (Prop NN), and oppose the mandatory life-without-parole sentencing for human trafficking of a minor — taking an abstain position on the latter instead. Commissioners also agreed to oppose Amendment 84 (mail ballot ID requirement), oppose the constitutional right to hunt and fish, and oppose Prop 132 (mandatory fentanyl sentencing), with Sheriff Kovalt detailing the unfunded-mandate burden on rural jails. Amendment 85 (plain-language ballot requirement) drew initial interest but ended in an oppose position after staff flagged conflicts with existing constitutional ballot language. Amendment 81 (law enforcement/federal immigration communication) was held pending the sheriff's further research.
